big: Dadi gets a call: 'Madam, your bank account will be blocked today. Please share the code sent to you.' She almost does. The code is the key to her money, and the caller is a thief.

lines: The caller knew my name and my bank. He sounded very polite.
Names and banks are easy to find or buy. Polite is part of the act. The rule is simple: never share the code, the PIN or the password with anyone.

title: Phone frauds
stops: Never share an OTP with anyone, even a bank officer
Approving a UPI collect request means you receive money
A fake link can steal your password or card details
A support agent may ask for a screen-sharing app
caps: A bank never needs your OTP. Whoever asks for it wants your money.
A collect request takes money out of your account when you approve it.
Phishing links lead to look-alike pages that copy what you type.
A screen-sharing app lets the fraudster see and control your phone.

intro: Four tricks, one goal: your approval.
rows: A fake link to get your password or card details
A request that looks like money coming in, but takes it out
The code that completes a payment in your name
A tool that lets a stranger run your phone
note: Money coming in never needs your PIN. If a screen asks for your PIN, you are paying.

q: A buyer on a marketplace says: 'I have sent you a request. Approve it with your PIN to receive the payment.' What is this?
opts: A normal way to receive money from a buyer
A refund from the marketplace seller
A collect fraud, where approving pays out
why: To receive money, a person needs to share only a UPI ID, and no PIN.
A bank does not ask customers to approve security checks with a PIN.
A genuine refund arrives on its own, with no PIN from the buyer.
Receiving money never needs a PIN, and approving a request pays the sender.

q: A caller says he is from Rohan's bank and needs the OTP to stop a fraud. What should Rohan do?
opts: Share the OTP, since the call is about safety
Hang up, and call the bank on its printed number
Share only half of the OTP digits
Ask the caller to send the same message again
why: The OTP lets the caller complete a payment in his name, so it must stay private.
A real bank never asks for an OTP, so hanging up and calling the printed number is safe.
Half a code can still help a fraudster, so he should share none of it.
Repeating the message adds nothing, since the request itself is the fraud.

q: A text says Meena's account is blocked and shows a link to 'update KYC'. What is the safest step?
opts: Ignore it, and open the bank's app herself
Click the link, since it came by text message
Reply with her card number to prove who she is
Forward the text to her contacts to warn them
why: A link in a text may lead to a fake page, so she should use the official app or site.
The text itself is the trick, so the link should not be opened at all.
Sharing her card number gives the fraudster what he came for.
Forwarding can spread the link and does not check whether it is real.

q: A 'support agent' asks Rohan to install a screen-sharing app to fix a payment problem. What is the risk?
opts: The app will speed up all of his payments
The bank will refund him much sooner
The agent can control his phone
The app will remove his old messages
why: A screen-sharing tool does nothing to speed up payments.
A bank does not ask customers to install such tools to process a refund.
Such tools give a stranger full view and control, including over banking apps.
Removing messages is not the aim. Access to his phone and money is.

pts: Never share an OTP, PIN or password. No real bank asks for them.
Money coming in never needs your PIN. If it asks for a PIN, you are paying.
Do not click links or install apps at a stranger's request.
